[[File:Paley.jpg|thumb|100px|Photograph of Paley's grave in The Old Banff Cemetery. The main gate is visible on the left.]]
'''Raymond Edward Alan Christopher Paley''' (7 January 1907 – 7 April 1933) was an [[England|English]] [[mathematician]] who made significant contributions to [[mathematical analysis]] before dying young in a skiing accident.

==Life==
Paley was born in [[Bournemouth, England]], the son of an artillery officer who died of tuberculosis before Paley was born. He was educated at [[Eton College]] as a [[King's Scholar]]{{r|jones}} and at [[Trinity College, Cambridge]].{{r|mactutor}} He became a [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|wrangler]] in 1928,{{r|hardy}} and with [[J. A. Todd]], he was one of two winners of the 1930 [[Smith's Prize]] examination.{{r|mactutor|hardy}}

He was elected a Research Fellow of Trinity College in 1930,{{r|times}} edging out Todd for the position,{{r|atiyah}} and continued at Cambridge as a postgraduate student, advised by [[John Edensor Littlewood]]. After the 1931 return of [[G. H. Hardy]] to Cambridge he participated in weekly joint seminars with the other students of Hardy and Littlewood.{{r|ricwil}} He traveled to the US in 1932 to work with [[Norbert Wiener]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and with [[George Pólya]] at [[Princeton University]],{{r|jones}} and as part of the same trip also planned to work with [[Lipót Fejér]] at a seminar in Chicago organized as part of the [[Century of Progress]] exposition.{{r|wiener}}

He was killed on 7 April 1933 in a skiing trip to the [[Canadian Rockies]], by an [[avalanche]] on [[Deception Pass (Alberta)|Deception Pass]].{{r|mactutor}}{{Quote|text=Paley, born in 1907, was one of the greatest stars in pure mathematics in Britain, whose young genius frightened even Hardy. Had he lived, he might well have turned into another Littlewood: his 26 papers, written mostly in collaboration with Littlewood, Zygmund, Wiener and Ursell, opened new areas in analysis.|title=Littlewood's Miscellany|author=[[Béla Bollobás]]|source=Foreword}}

==Contributions==
Paley's contributions include the following.
*His mathematical research with Littlewood began in 1929, with his work towards a fellowship at Trinity, and Hardy writes that "Littlewood's influence dominates nearly all his earliest work".{{r|hardy}} Their work became the foundation for [[Littlewood–Paley theory]], an application of real-variable techniques in [[complex analysis]].{{r|stein|fjw}}{{ran|a}} 
*The Walsh–Paley numeration, a standard method for indexing the [[Walsh function]]s, came from a 1932 suggestion of Paley.{{r|trakhtman}}{{ran|b}}
*Paley collaborated with [[Antoni Zygmund]] on [[Fourier series]],{{r|mactutor}} continuing the work on this topic that he had already done with Littlewood.{{r|wiener}} His work in this area also led to the [[Paley–Zygmund inequality]] in [[probability theory]].{{r|ghosh}}{{ran|c}}
*In a 1933 paper, he published the [[Paley construction]] for [[Hadamard matrix|Hadamard matrices]].{{r|macslo}}{{ran|d}} In the same paper, he first formulated the [[Hadamard conjecture]] on the sizes of matrices for which Hadamard matrices exist.{{r|hedwal}} The [[Paley graph]]s and Paley [[Tournament (graph theory)|tournaments]] in [[graph theory]] are closely related, although they do not appear explicitly in this work.{{r|jones}} In the context of [[compressed sensing]], [[Frame (linear algebra)|frames]] (partial bases of [[Hilbert space]]s) derived from this construction have been called "Paley equiangular tight frames".{{r|mixon|renes}}
*His collaboration with [[Norbert Wiener]] included the [[Paley–Wiener theorem]] in [[harmonic analysis]].{{r|rudin}} Paley was originally selected as the 1934 [[American Mathematical Society]] Colloquium Lecturer; after his death, Wiener replaced him as speaker, and spoke on their joint work,{{r|mactutor}} which was published as a book.{{ran|e}}

==Selected publications==
For the short span of his research career, Paley was very productive; Hardy lists 26 of Paley's publications,{{r|hardy}} and more were published posthumously. These publications include:
